The 24-centimeter neonates are born fully formed and immediately capable of independent foraging, a life-history strategy that minimizes the period of vulnerability to predation while maximizing the use of warm, productive inshore waters during the early juvenile stage.

Females, by contrast, do not attain sexual maturity until they reach a total length of approximately 55 centimeters [Lp = approximately 55 centimeters], at which stage ovarian follicles begin to develop and ovulation becomes possible. This offset in maturation size is ecologically significant, as it allows males to begin participating in reproductive activities while still growing, whereas females must invest additional somatic resources before diverting energy toward gamete production.
